adversarial_test_results.prompt: For most of the nineteenth century the northern fisheries depended on a chain of lighthouses whose keepers recorded weather, shipping and bird migrations in leather-bound journals. Historians long treated the journals as a curiosity, useful mainly for anecdotes about storms and wrecks. A team at the coastal archive has now digitised four decades of entries from eleven stations and compared them with naval logs and newspaper reports. The work took longer than expected, because many entries were written in a shorthand the volunteers had to learn, and gaps of weeks or months appear wherever a keeper fell ill or moved away. Two of the eleven stations kept their journals in duplicate, which allowed the team to check for copying errors, while the rest survive in a single hand. The comparison revealed a pattern nobody had looked for: the dates of the spring herring runs drifted northward by roughly nine days between 1850 and 1890, and the keepers noted the change decades before the fisheries inspectors did. The journals also recorded unusual numbers of stranded seabirds after the coldest winters, a correlation oceanographers have since confirmed with modern survey data. None of the keepers understood the forces behind the patterns they described, and the inspectors who read their reports dismissed the observations as the complaints of lonely men. That dismissal, the team argues, delayed the adoption of seasonal fishing limits by almost thirty years. The journals themselves were nearly lost: damp, mould and a fire in 1931 destroyed perhaps half of the volumes, and the survivors sat in unheated storerooms until a librarian in Aberdeen began cataloguing them in the 1970s. The report, published last month, calls for the remaining volumes to be conserved and made available to researchers, and it recommends photographing each page at high resolution and linking the images to the naval logs, so future historians can trace individual voyages across both sources. These findings may also interest climatologists, since the keepers' notes on ice and wind are among the few continuous records from the period.
